name: Vincentian Creole English
sweep_summary: vinc1243 is not in the catalog. Two title hits: (1) Hill 2019 (Folia Linguistica Historica) is a false hit — Glottolog's record says the Vincentian tag is a 'computerized assignment from \"apparent\"'; the abstract (Crossref/S2) is about the Prosodic Change Hypothesis in historical sound change, nothing on Vincentian; closed access, priority none. (2) Prescod 2006 (STUF 59(2):191-210) was obtained and read in the author's own open French translation on HAL (hal-01115827; HAL's Anubis bot-wall meant the file was pulled from the Wayback snapshot;. It is mostly post-lexical (intensity/F0 disambiguation of 8 utterance pairs in Praat); at word level it says only that lexical stress distinguishes N/V pairs as in English, that inter-syllable intensity differences are very small, and that the pitch-contrasted pair bròdà/brôdà both bear initial stress — no general placement rule. The English original (paywalled De Gruyter) remains unread, priority medium. Best first-hand statement found: Prescod's APiCS survey chapter (2013, §4 Phonology): 'In polysyllabic words, stress is generally assigned to the first syllable..., failing which, stress falls on the syllable that contains a long vowel or a diphthong... and on the syllable before -shan and -zan' — initial default with weight- and suffix-driven overrides; this would be the deciding source if a catalog record is created. new_statements.quote: In polysyllabic words, stress is generally assigned to the first syllable (cf. Prescod 2006: 61), failing which, stress falls on the syllable that contains a long vowel or a diphthong: teliˈfoon 'telephone' and on the syllable before -shan and -zan: badaˈreishan 'trouble', teliˈvizan 'television'.
new_statements.citation: Prescod, Paula (2013). Vincentian Creole. In Michaelis, Susanne Maria, Maurer, Philippe, Haspelmath, Martin & Huber, Magnus (eds), The survey of pidgin and creole languages, vol. 1: English-based and Dutch-based languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press; APiCS Online survey chapter 7 (https://apics-online.info/surveys/7), section 4 'Phonology'.
new_statements.locator: APiCS Online survey chapter 7, §4 Phonology, last paragraph (syllable structure / stress)
new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the language's principal describer (native speaker, author of the only instrumental prosody study). Default word stress is initial in polysyllables; this default is overridden by syllable weight (a long vowel or diphthong attracts stress, e.g. teliˈfoon) and by the suffixes -shan/-zan, which place stress on the immediately pre-suffixal syllable (badaˈreishan, teliˈvizan). So: weight-sensitive, morphologically conditioned stress with an initial default — not a fixed-position system; noun/verb pairs can also be stress-distinguished (Prescod 2006, p. 2 of the HAL version), and pitch contour rather than intensity separates some polysyllabic lexical pairs (bròdà/brôdà).

sources.citation: Prescod, Paula (2006). Stress assignment and functions of pitch in Vincentian Creole. In Parth Bhatt & Ingo Plag (eds), Stress, tone and intonation in creole and contact languages. STUF - Sprachtypologie und Universalienforschung 59(2): 191-210. [Read in the author's own French translation, 'Accentuation et fonctions de mélodie en créole vincentien', HAL hal-01115827, 24 pp.]
sources.quote: « Comme en anglais, non seulement peut-on employer l'accent lexical démarcatif pour différencier un item nominal d'un item verbal tel que dans taamentN et taamentV » (p. 2) … « Nos mesures acoustiques affirment qu'en VinC, il y a très peu de différence d'intensité entre les syllabes au niveau lexical. […] dans des paires polysyllabiques, ni la durée ni l'intensité ne semblent avoir d'effet sur l'interprétation sémantique. […] les deux mots portent l'accent tonique sur la première syllabe » (p. 4; bròdà 'frère (famille)' vs brôdà 'frère (ordre religieux)')
sources.locator: HAL French version p. 2 (§1 Introduction) and p. 4 (§2.2 'Le rôle des suprasegmentaux dans l'identification des paires minimales'); ≈ STUF pp. 192-195 of the English original
sources.note: Translation: 'As in English, demarcative lexical stress can be used to distinguish a nominal from a verbal item, as in taament(N)/taament(V) "torment" … Our acoustic measurements confirm that in VinC there is very little intensity difference between syllables at the lexical level. […] in polysyllabic pairs neither duration nor intensity seems to affect semantic interpretation […] both words carry stress on the first syllable' (bròdà 'brother (kin)' vs brôdà 'brother (religious order)', distinguished by pitch contour, after Devonish 1989).
